questions.question: Why do real protocols run the raw Diffie–Hellman shared secret through a KDF like HKDF?
options: To turn shared secret bytes into uniform keys and bind them to protocol context
To hide the handshake messages from passive observers
To make Diffie–Hellman faster by shortening the exponentiation
To avoid needing any randomness in the protocol
questions.explanation: HKDF produces key material with the right size and distribution, and lets you safely incorporate context (salt/info/transcript) into derived keys.

questions.question: What is the main risk if an AEAD key is ever used with the same nonce twice?
options: Nothing breaks as long as the plaintexts are different
It can enable plaintext recovery and/or message forgery, depending on the AEAD
Only performance degrades; security is unchanged
Only authentication breaks; confidentiality remains intact
questions.explanation: Nonce reuse is catastrophic for most AEADs (e.g., stream-cipher based modes and GCM), often breaking confidentiality and sometimes integrity too.

questions.question: In Noise, what does the handshake hash h (updated by mix_hash) represent?
options: A commitment to the exact bytes sent/received so far in the handshake
A long-term shared secret stored across connections
A checksum that only detects accidental network corruption
A hash of the final application data stream
questions.explanation: h is a transcript hash: it commits to the handshake messages so both parties can bind key derivation and AEAD associated data to what was actually exchanged.

questions.question: What does mix_key do when new secret material (like a DH output) becomes available?
options: It replaces the handshake hash h with a hash of the new secret
It updates the chaining key ck via HKDF and produces a derived key for encryption
It encrypts the secret and appends it to the handshake transcript
It signs the secret using a static private key
questions.explanation: mix_key feeds the secret into HKDF with ck as salt, producing a new ck and a temporary key used by the handshake's encrypt-and-hash steps.

questions.question: Why does Noise hash the ciphertext (including the tag) into the transcript after encrypting a handshake payload?
options: So both sides commit to the exact encrypted bytes, preventing transcript splicing and desynchronization
So the payload can be decrypted without the key
So the payload becomes smaller on the wire
So the protocol can skip AEAD associated data
questions.explanation: Encrypt-and-hash binds the encrypted payload into h, ensuring both parties agree on the same transcript and preventing attackers from swapping or replaying handshake fragments.

questions.question: If you use the NN pattern in a setting that requires server authentication, what attack is enabled?
options: A man-in-the-middle can establish two separate handshakes and relay traffic between them
A passive eavesdropper can decrypt traffic without participating
The AEAD tag can be forged without knowing the key
Forward secrecy is guaranteed even if static keys are compromised
questions.explanation: NN provides confidentiality but no authentication, so an active attacker can impersonate each side to the other and relay messages.

questions.question: Why does Noise split transport keys into per-direction tx/rx keys instead of using one key for both directions?
options: To reduce the number of keys and simplify the state machine
To avoid nonce collisions, reflection issues, and key/nonce reuse across directions
Because HKDF can only output one key at a time
Because AEAD requires two independent secrets to work
questions.explanation: Per-direction keys let each side maintain its own nonce counter safely and prevent cross-direction replay/reflection patterns that can arise with shared keys.

questions.question: After the handshake completes, what should transport encryption use?
options: The last handshake encryption key k, reused for all application data
Only the transcript hash h, used as the encryption key
The split transport keys derived from ck (one for each direction)
The raw DH shared secret directly, without a KDF
questions.explanation: Noise derives transport keys from the final chaining key and then uses those per-direction keys for application data; handshake keys are transient and scoped to the handshake.
